Reviewer #3:

In this paper, the authors analyze the effects that polymorphic TE insertions have on chromatin states in Drosophila. This paper is an extension of a previous study that was limited by the fact that the effect of polymorphic TE insertions could not be determined since only one reference was used (from ModEncode, for example). In this paper, the authors explicitly examine the effects of TE insertion polymorphism on variation in repressed chromatin signatures within the genome. This is an important contribution to the field and is very well written.

My major concern, which I will point out specifically in several places, is that the representation of the data limits the reader’s ability to understand the variation in the signal. In particular, many of the figures compress the data into box plots, where this compression is not appropriate. I will alert the authors to this paper:

"Beyond Bar and Line Graphs: Time for a New Data Presentation Paradigm". While the authors might think this concern is nitpicky, I don't think so. The authors are aiming for a high-profile paper and the readers should be able to see the structure of the underlying data and variation. Not all figures are at issue, but some can be revised.

The article is lacking reference to the work of the Kalmykova lab. In particular, the article must cite Shpiz et al. Euchromatic transposon insertions trigger […] This paper is an important contribution to the field.

Subsection “Euchromatic TEs exhibit extensive epigenetic effects on adjacent sequences”, second paragraph: It would be worth illuminating in the text the interesting observation in Figure 1 that embryos show these effects most strongly.

Subsection “Euchromatic TEs exhibit extensive epigenetic effects on adjacent sequences”, fourth paragraph: It is a little awkward to say "homologous sequences that lack nearby TEs." I think the authors mean "with corresponding alleles lacking the TE insertion."

Subsection “Euchromatic TEs exhibit extensive epigenetic effects on adjacent sequences”, fourth paragraph: Since the metrics "extent of spread" and "% increase in H3K9me" are used throughout, please exactly define these metrics here, not just in the Methods.

Subsection “Euchromatic TEs exhibit extensive epigenetic effects on adjacent sequences”, fourth paragraph: Please exactly define the characteristic: "associated with enrichment for H3K9me2 in at least 1 kb". Likewise, please define how the extent of spreading is defined (what is the cutoff for spread).

Figure 2 legend. Please clarify in the legend that these are TE insertion alleles that are absent in the other strain.

Subsection “TE families of LTR-type and targeted by piRNAs show stronger epigenetic effects”: There is a suggestion that LTRs have stronger effects. This is demonstrated in several ways, but I don't follow the statistics:

1) Subsection “TE families of LTR-type and targeted by piRNAs show stronger epigenetic effects”, second paragraph: There is suggestion of enrichment with several statements such as "eight of 11 TE families with over half of insertions […] are LTR-type" Is this enrichment significant, given there are more LTR families? A Fisher's exact would be suitable here. A similar point can be made about the next sentence.

2)They perform a statistical test of this phenomenon (subsection “TE families of LTR-type and targeted by piRNAs show stronger epigenetic effects”, second paragraph), but it is not clear the test is appropriate. Here, they seem to be binning all LTRs (I could be wrong) but this Mann-Whitney U result may be solely driven by one abundant LTR family, such as copia or roo. The authors should provide a more convincing case that LTRs really exert a stronger effect, in general, instead of this being driven by some families. This could be done in an ANOVA framework, where the effect of TE class is explicitly tested, in contrast to family level effects.

Subsection “TE families of LTR-type and targeted by piRNAs show stronger epigenetic effects”, third paragraph: "It is worth noting […]" I don't understand this sentence. It appears that they are saying that there are no differences, between strains, in piRNA abundance for each given family. Is that correct? Then why are P-values indicated for two genotypes, sense such a test between two strains would have one P value?

Figure 5 is an example of data compression with bar charts that is not appropriate. First, frequency should not be binned in this manner. Such binning is arbitrary and masks the underlying data. Please plot these values continuously. In addition, for 5B and 5C, plot the Y axis continuously for each TE insertion.

Also, in regard to the analysis of population frequencies, this analysis seems completely confounded by the previously reported family level effects and copia number effects. For example, copia elements (LTRs, with large copia number) may also have low frequencies for other reasons that have nothing to do with the effect they exert on local chromatin. I imagine there are two ways to deal with this. 1) All contrasts must control for within family effects. For example, the test should be: Do copia elements with a stronger chromatin effect have lower frequencies than other copia elements? Do roo elements with a stronger chromatin effect have lower frequencies than other roo elements? The family level effects must be accounted for. 2) A formal way to do this would be to directly model population frequency and perform a multiple logistic regression where family effects and chromatin effects are evaluated for their capacity to predict frequencies in the population. This way, family effects and chromatin effects can be explicitly measured and evaluated.

Right now, this binning approach is not appropriate.

Subsection “Epigenetic effects of TEs result in differential epigenetic states of adjacent coding genes”. Similar data compression by binning for the expression analysis is not appropriate. The Fisher's exact test approach in Table 2 doesn't seem appropriate. There is a very nice paired structure to these data that can simply be measured as the difference in RPKM between alleles with a TE and alleles without a TE. Then, a scatter plot can be shown to demonstrate the degree to which chromatin effects are predictive of gene expression differences. Here, the X-axis would be some continuous measure of chromatin effect and the Y-axis would be the measured effect on gene expression. Such a scatter plot is essential for the reader to evaluate the nature of these data. These bins do not allow the reader to understand what is going on.

Figure 7. It seems a binomial test would show 7B (proportion of TE spread) significant, but not for the rest of 7B. Please provide P values for a test of more dots above the diagonal than below the diagonal in 7B.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Pervasive epigenetic effects of Drosophila euchromatic transposable elements impact their evolution" for further consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Detlef Weigel (Senior Editor) and three reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

As requested by Reviewer #1, please integrate other previous findings better.

As requested by Reviewer #3, please address points 1, 3, and 4 (or explain why this is not a good idea).

The paper is excellent: we just think it would be further improved with relatively little effort.

Reviewer #1:

I'm happy with your response to my comments with one exception: just adding a bunch of plant references at one point in the Introduction is not enough. Sure, the authors get the citation count credit they deserve, but in the name of scholarship you should do better.

What struck me when I read your paper is how closely it parallels findings in plants, and I think your paper would improve if you made this clear.

For example, the spreading of silencing has been shown several times in plants, and there is also strong evidence that selection depends on this. Population frequencies appear to be low, and the recent Arabidopsis paper by Colot's group clearly showed that insertions are uniform, but that selection removes them so that older (more frequent) TEs cluster around the centromeres.

I know it is a pain to do this, but there are several places in both Introduction and Discussion where you could note these similarities. It would really improve the paper, and would be a service to a field that is too often is organism-limited.

Someone needs to spend a day in a coffee house with a (virtual) stack of papers and a laptop. This is not too much to ask.

With respect to estimating the age of TEs, I understand that you cannot sequence the interior of the TE, but did you try the haplotype sharing? I think it could be more powerful than you suggest. This is real work, however, and I'm fine with your dropping the section instead.

Reviewer #2:

The authors have done a thorough job responding to the reviewers' comments. I heartily endorse publication in eLife.

Reviewer #3:

This is the second version of this article that I have read. The results are very interesting and important, but I feel the argument simplifies some complexity that should be more acknowledged. The authors have addressed many of my concerns, but, as in my first review, I will ask that the authors improve the presentation to allow readers to have a more clear understanding of the underlying complexities.

1) With regard to the definition of extent of spread, I am still slightly confused. The authors do a good job and provide a graphical representation of these definitions, but by "farthest window", how do they deal with values on one side being larger than values on the other side. Suppose the extent of spread to the left is 15 kb and the extent of spread to the right is 6 kb. Is a max function used such that 15 kb is the defined extent? Please be exact and precise in this definition.

2) Introduction, last paragraph, and elsewhere, I think there should be a bit more of a hedge on the conclusion that selection is determining the patterns. Therefore, a sentence like "we observed stronger selection against TE insertions" would preferably be "we find evidence that stronger selection against TE insertions"

3) This is my most significant comment. I am still confused about the expression analysis.

First, from Table 3, it appears this effect is only observed in one strain. In fact, for TEs in RAL315 (top set of genes in Table 2), the odds ratio is 0.95, the opposite expected. Therefore, it is not clear to me that one can argue that this result is straightforward. The authors should be upfront about this strain effect. It's interesting! But it certainly makes the story more complex and reduces the strength of their broader conclusion.

Second, Table 3 can still be improved. For one, the Fisher's Exact test is being performed against the background genes (with respect to sign of effect of enrichment and expression between the two strains), but the way it is presented, the nature of values in the 2X2 table is cryptic. From first look, one might think that the four values in each row are members of the 2X2 table. Now, this is not the correct interpretation, but I encourage the authors to make this clearer. In particular, why not just provide the four different 2X2 tables? This is also made confusing from the fact that, it appears, the numbers are wrong in the example below the table. By my count, for the RAL315 TEs, 56 is the value in the focal cell (H3K9me2 higher in 315, Higher expression in 360), but the values of the other cells (based on the text below) should sum to 121, correct? But, by my count, the rest of the genes with the other states add to 177 (75+56+46). I am sorry if I am wrong, but I guess I am still confused. I do think that presentation of the actual 2X2 tables that go into the FET would be best.

In light of these issues, I am still not convinced that Fisher's exacts tests of this kind are the best way to present the data. In my last review, I had requested a figure more like Figure 7 and I appreciate the authors providing it. However, it is clear from this new figure that the effect that these TEs have on expression, via H3K9me2, is complicated. For example, from the scatter plots for RAL315 TE insertions, there are 131 genes with TE inserts that have higher H3K9me2 in RAL315. However, among these genes, most (75) show a higher level of expression in 315 – the opposite pattern expected. It is also appears from these scatterplots that there is perhaps no correlation between fold H3K9me2 enrichment differences and differences in expression. This is a very interesting and extremely important complexity that must be made evident to the reader. Therefore, I request that these scatter plots be provided in the main figures with a revised version of Table 3 and a correlation coefficient be provided for these scatter plots.

4) The authors have done a good job controlling for the non-independent effects of family and spread of H3K9me in predicting TE insertion frequency. This is evident in their Methods (subsection “TE population frequency analysis”). However, Table 2 doesn't provide the jointly estimated regression coefficient for family. It just provides regression coefficients and p-values for extent and magnitude of spread. Please provide results from the full models, where regression coefficients were jointly estimated for epigenetic and family effects.

claims.source: Using modEncode ChIP-seq data generated from the Oregon-R strain, we observed that sequences flanking euchromatic TEs are also enriched for another key heterochromatic histone modification (H3K9me2) and HP1a, while depleted for 'active' histone modifications H3K4me2 and H3K4me3, which are enriched at transcribing promoters (Kouzarides, 2007; Kharchenko et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Enrichment for repressive epigenetic marks around TEs is strongest at the embryonic stage and weaker at later developmental stages.
claims.source: Interestingly, enrichment for repressive epigenetic marks around TEs is strongest at the embryonic stage and weaker at later developmental stages, consistent with our previous study of only H3K9me3 (Lee 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode data at different developmental stages and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The presence of TEs correlated with substantially higher H3K9me2 enrichment in RAL315 and RAL360 strains.
claims.source: The presence of TEs correlated with substantially higher H3K9me2 enrichment (Figure 2), which strongly supports the conclusion that these repressive mark enrichments are due to TE insertions, and not pre-existing epigenetic states.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparing H3K9me2 enrichment at homologous sequences with and without TEs, shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The enrichment of repressive marks around TEs is due to TE insertions, and not pre-existing epigenetic states.
claims.source: The presence of TEs correlated with substantially higher H3K9me2 enrichment (Figure 2), which strongly supports the conclusion that these repressive mark enrichments are due to TE insertions, and not pre-existing epigenetic states.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of homologous sequences with and without TEs.

claims.claim: 54.2% of 419 euchromatic TEs analyzed were associated with enrichment for H3K9me2 in at least 1 kb of adjacent sequences.
claims.source: Surprisingly, more than half of the euchromatic TEs (54.2% of 419 TEs analyzed) were associated with enrichment for H3K9me2 in at least 1 kb of adjacent sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis of RAL315 and RAL360 strains.

claims.claim: The TE-induced spreading of H3K9me2 in flanking sequence extended for a mean of 4.50 kb (standard deviation 4.59 kb).
claims.source: The TE-induced spreading of H3K9me2 in flanking sequence extended for a mean of 4.50 kb (standard deviation 4.59 kb), and an average of 79.8% increase in H3K9me2 enrichment at the TE insertion site (standard deviation 78.8%, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claims.claim: TEs cause an average of 79.8% increase in H3K9me2 enrichment at the TE insertion site (standard deviation 78.8%).
claims.source: The TE-induced spreading of H3K9me2 in flanking sequence extended for a mean of 4.50 kb (standard deviation 4.59 kb), and an average of 79.8% increase in H3K9me2 enrichment at the TE insertion site (standard deviation 78.8%, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claims.claim: TEs associated with H3K9me2 enrichment at flanking sequences are not concentrated around pericentromeric or subtelomeric heterochromatin.
claims.source: Our analysis focused on regions far from these heterochromatic regions, and showed that TEs associated with H3K9me2 enrichment at flanking sequences are not concentrated around pericentromeric or subtelomeric heterochromatin (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Local repeat density does not differ between TEs that are or are not associated with H3K9me2 spreading.
claims.source: Also, local repeat density does not differ between TEs that are or are not associated with H3K9me2 spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.55).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of local repeat density.

claims.claim: There are no correlations between the extent or magnitude of TE's epigenetic effects and local repeat density.
claims.source: Similarly, we observed no correlations between the extent or magnitude of TE's epigenetic effects and local repeat density (Spearman rank correlation test, p=0.81 (repeat density vs extent of H3K9me2 spread), 0.65 (repeat density vs % increase in H3K9me2)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Epigenetic influences of TEs are not restricted to specific genomic locations or contexts, and can be observed across diverse euchromatic regions.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that epigenetic influences of TEs are not restricted to specific genomic locations or contexts, and can be observed across diverse euchromatic regions.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of association with proximity to heterochromatin or local repeat density.

claims.claim: There is substantial variation in the epigenetic effects of insertions from different TE families.
claims.source: While our results demonstrate that euchromatic TEs have widespread epigenetic effects in D. melanogaster, we also found that the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions vary significantly. In particular, there is substantial variation in the epigenetic effects of insertions from different TE families (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3 comparing different TE families.

claims.claim: LTR-type TE families show a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to other types of TEs.
claims.source: Indeed, LTR-type TE families show a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to other types of TEs (Mann-Whitney U test p=0.00047, median: 0.547 (LTR) vs 0.352 (others), Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: TE families targeted by more piRNAs show more extensive H3K9me2 spreading and enrichment in flanking sequences.
claims.source: Consistently, we observed that TE families targeted by more piRNAs show more extensive H3K9me2 spreading and enrichment in flanking sequences (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: There is no difference in the amount of piRNAs targeting LTR-type TEs compared to other major types of TEs.
claims.source: It is worth noting that there is no difference in the amount of piRNAs targeting LTR-type TEs compared to other major types of TEs (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.19 (wK) and 0.39 (w1118)), suggesting that the observed correlation between the amount of piRNAs and TE's epigenetic effects was unlikely solely driven by stronger epigenetic effects of LTR-type TE families.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of piRNA amounts.

claims.claim: There are no significant associations between the epigenetic effects of TEs and targeting by endo-siRNAs.
claims.source: On the other hand, we did not find significant associations between the epigenetic effects of TEs and targeting by endo-siRNAs (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: TE families with higher copy numbers have larger proportions of insertions with epigenetic effects.
claims.source: Supporting this prediction, TE families with higher copy numbers in a large sample of African flies (Kofler et al., 2015) have larger proportions of insertions with epigenetic effects (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: Only 31.5% of TE insertions present in either RAL315 or RAL360 were found in the Zambian population.
claims.source: Consistent with previous genome-wide observations that most TE insertions have low population frequencies in D. melanogaster (González et al., 2008; Kofler et al., 2012, 2015; Cridland et al., 2013), only 31.5% of TE insertions present in either of the two DGRP strains analyzed were found in the Zambian population, and these TEs displayed very low population frequencies (0.54% (first quartile), 0.56% (median), 1.61% (third quartile), Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by population genomic analysis of Zambian flies.

claims.claim: TEs found in the Zambian population displayed very low population frequencies (0.54% first quartile, 0.56% median, 1.61% third quartile).
claims.source: Consistent with previous genome-wide observations that most TE insertions have low population frequencies in D. melanogaster (González et al., 2008; Kofler et al., 2012, 2015; Cridland et al., 2013), only 31.5% of TE insertions present in either of the two DGRP strains analyzed were found in the Zambian population, and these TEs displayed very low population frequencies (0.54% (first quartile), 0.56% (median), 1.61% (third quartile), Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by population frequency analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 compared to high frequency TEs.
claims.source: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 (Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.039, odds ratio = 1.58, Figure 5A), led to more extensive spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.011, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.014, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Low frequency TEs led to more extensive spreading of H3K9me2 compared to high frequency TEs.
claims.source: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 (Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.039, odds ratio = 1.58, Figure 5A), led to more extensive spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.011, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.014, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Low frequency TEs resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to high frequency TEs.
claims.source: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 (Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.039, odds ratio = 1.58, Figure 5A), led to more extensive spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.011, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.014, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: There are significant negative correlations between the strength of a TE's epigenetic effects and its population frequency.
claims.source: Consistently, by analyzing the population frequencies of individual TE insertions, we observed significant negative correlations between the strength of a TE's epigenetic effects and its population frequency (Spearman rank ρ = −0.15 (extent of H3K9me2 spread) and −0.14 increase in H3K9me2), p<0.005 for both, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Recombination rates do not differ between TEs with or without spreading of H3K9me2.
claims.source: However, we observed that recombination rates do not differ between TEs with or without spreading of H3K9me2 (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.83).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of recombination rates.

claims.claim: Neither the extent of H3K9me2 spread nor the increase in H3K9me2 enrichment in flanking sequences was correlated with the local recombination rate for individual TE insertions.
claims.source: Similarly, neither the extent of H3K9me2 spread nor the increase in H3K9me2 enrichment in flanking sequences was correlated with the local recombination rate for individual TE insertions (Spearman rank correlation test, p=0.62 (recombination rate vs extent of H3K9me2 spread) and 0.55 (recombination rate vs % increase in H3K9me2 enrichment)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Genes in proximity to TEs are more enriched for H3K9me2 within each of the two strains analyzed.
claims.source: Within each of the two strains analyzed, genes in proximity to TEs are more enriched for H3K9me2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations (Lee 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Genes with adjacent TEs have significantly higher, positive z-scores compared to genes distant from TEs in both strains.
claims.source: As expected, genes with adjacent TEs in either strain have significantly higher, positive z-scores compared to genes distant from TEs in both strains (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by z-score analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: For all categories of genes within 10 kb from TEs, z-scores are significantly higher for genes whose neighboring TEs exhibit H3K9me2 spreading.
claims.source: For all categories of genes within 10 kb from TEs, z-scores are significantly higher for genes whose neighboring TEs exhibit H3K9me2 spreading (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: There are significant positive correlations between the z-scores of genes and the extent of epigenetic effects from the nearest TEs.
claims.source: Consistently, there are significant positive correlations between the z-scores of genes and the extent of epigenetic effects from the nearest TEs (vs. the extent of H3K9me2 spread: Spearman rank ρ = 0.31, p<10−15; vs. % increase in H3K9me2 enrichment: Spearman rank ρ = 0.30, p<10−15).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Genes whose nearest TEs did not exhibit epigenetic effects have similar z-scores to genes without TEs within 10 kb.
claims.source: It is worth noting that genes whose nearest TEs did not exhibit epigenetic effects have similar z-scores to genes without TEs within 10 kb (dashed line, Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The spread of repressive epigenetic marks from euchromatic TEs leads to substantial epigenetic differences at homologous alleles of adjacent coding genes.
claims.source: These observations demonstrate that the spread of repressive epigenetic marks from euchromatic TEs leads to substantial epigenetic differences at homologous alleles of adjacent coding genes.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the z-score analysis comparing homologous alleles.

claims.claim: Among genes adjacent to TEs with epigenetic effects, those whose nearest TEs were absent in the Zambian population have significantly higher z-scores than genes adjacent to high frequency TEs.
claims.source: Among these genes, those whose nearest TEs were absent in the Zambian population ('low frequency' TEs, see above) have significantly higher z-scores than genes adjacent to 'high frequency' TEs (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.0019, median: 0.95 (genes near low frequency TEs) vs 0.32 (genes near high frequency TEs)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison.

claims.claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the z-score of a gene and the population frequency of its nearest TE.
claims.source: Consistently, there is a significant negative correlation between the z-score of a gene and the population frequency of its nearest TE (Spearman rank ρ = −0.18, p<10−3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Within either strain, there are significant negative correlations between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels for genes within 10 kb of TEs.
claims.source: Within either strain, there are indeed significant negative correlations between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels for genes within 10 kb of TEs (Spearman rank ρ = −0.35 (RAL315) and −0.33 (RAL360), p<10−16 for both).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: There is an excess number of genes that support the influence of TE's epigenetic effects on gene expression for genes with TEs within 10 kb when compared to other genes in the genome.
claims.source: We found an excess number of genes that support the influence of TE's epigenetic effects on gene expression (higher H3K9me2 enrichment and lower expression of alleles with adjacent TEs, shaded green area in Figure 7A) for genes with TEs within 10 kb when compared to other genes in the genome (Figure 7B, upper 2 × 2 Tables).
claims.evidence: This is supported by contingency table analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Restricting the analysis to TEs with epigenetic effects produced an even larger proportion of genes whose TE-neighboring alleles have higher H3K9me2 enrichment and lower expression.
claims.source: Restricting the analysis to TEs with epigenetic effects produced an even larger proportion of genes whose TE-neighboring alleles have higher H3K9me2 enrichment and lower expression (Figure 7B, bottom 2 × 2 Tables).
claims.evidence: This is supported by contingency table analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The excess number of genes supporting TE-induced epigenetic effects on expression was mainly observed for one of the two strains analyzed (RAL360).
claims.source: Intriguingly, the excess number of genes supporting TE-induced epigenetic effects on expression was mainly observed for one of the two strains analyzed (RAL360).
claims.evidence: This is observed from the contingency table analysis in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: There is a weak, but significant, negative correlation between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes without TEs.
claims.source: Furthermore, while we found a weak, but significant, negative correlation between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes without TEs (Spearman rank ρ = −0.035, p=0.0084), there are no such correlations observed for genes with TEs within 10 kb (Spearman rank test p=0. 57 (RAL315) and 0.16 (RAL360)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: There are no correlations between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes with TEs within 10 kb.
claims.source: Furthermore, while we found a weak, but significant, negative correlation between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes without TEs (Spearman rank ρ = −0.035, p=0.0084), there are no such correlations observed for genes with TEs within 10 kb (Spearman rank test p=0. 57 (RAL315) and 0.16 (RAL360)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claims.claim: D. simulans diverged from D. melanogaster four million years ago.
claims.source: D. simulans diverged from D. melanogaster only four million years ago (Obbard et al., 2012), yet is widely observed to harbor fewer TE insertions compared to D. melanogaster (Dowsett and Young, 1982; Vieira et al., 1999; Vieira and Biémont, 2004; Kofler et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a phylogenetic study.

claims.claim: D. simulans is widely observed to harbor fewer TE insertions compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: D. simulans diverged from D. melanogaster only four million years ago (Obbard et al., 2012), yet is widely observed to harbor fewer TE insertions compared to D. melanogaster (Dowsett and Young, 1982; Vieira et al., 1999; Vieira and Biémont, 2004; Kofler et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple comparative studies.

claims.claim: Strong H3K9me2 enrichment is observed in sequences flanking TEs in D. simulans.
claims.source: Similar to D. melanogaster, we observed strong H3K9me2 enrichment in sequences flanking TEs (Figure 8A), and genes adjacent to TEs have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes distant from TEs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis in D. simulans shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: In D. simulans, genes adjacent to TEs have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes distant from TEs.
claims.source: Similar to D. melanogaster, we observed strong H3K9me2 enrichment in sequences flanking TEs (Figure 8A), and genes adjacent to TEs have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes distant from TEs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In D. simulans, genes adjacent to TEs with epigenetic effects have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes adjacent to TEs without epigenetic effects.
claims.source: Furthermore, genes adjacent to TEs with epigenetic effects (see below) have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes adjacent to TEs without epigenetic effects (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: For genes within 10 kb of TEs in D. simulans, there is a strong negative correlation between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels.
claims.source: For genes within 10 kb of TEs, there is also a strong negative correlation between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels (Spearman rank ρ = −0.45, p<10−16), supporting a functional consequence of H3K9me2 enrichment in D. simulans.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data in D. simulans.

claims.claim: There are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread.
claims.source: While there are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread (paired MWU test, p=0.67), TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (paired MWU test, p=0.013), and a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment (paired MWU test, p=0.035; Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: While there are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread (paired MWU test, p=0.67), TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (paired MWU test, p=0.013), and a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment (paired MWU test, p=0.035; Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: TE families in D. simulans display a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: While there are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread (paired MWU test, p=0.67), TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (paired MWU test, p=0.013), and a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment (paired MWU test, p=0.035; Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: TEs in D. simulans exhibit stronger epigenetic effects on flanking sequences compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that TEs in D. simulans exhibit stronger epigenetic effects on flanking sequences compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative analysis between the two species.

claims.claim: D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Consistent with previous quantitation of simple repeat content using orthogonal approaches (melting curves [Lohe and Brutlag, 1987] or flow cytometry [Bosco et al., 2007]), we observed lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster (Figure 9A, ANOVA p-value=0.00013 (species) and <10−6 (library preparation method)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by K-mer analysis shown in Figure 9A and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: 40 known Su(var) genes as a group have higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Compared to other genes in the genome, 40 known Su(var)s, as a group, have higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<10−6, Figure 9B; also see Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Figure 9—source data 1 for individual genes included in the analysis).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Su(var)3–9 showed significantly higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Among these dosage-dependent Su(var)s/E(var)s, Su(var)3–9 showed significantly higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats and higher expression of Su(var)s compared to D. melanogaster, both of which could account for the stronger epigenetic effects of TEs observed in D. simulans.
claims.source: Overall, we found that D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats and higher expression of Su(var)s compared to D. melanogaster, both of which could account for the stronger epigenetic effects of TEs observed in D. simulans.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of heterochromatic DNA content and Su(var) expression.

claims.claim: More than half of euchromatic TEs analyzed are associated with at least 1 kb spread of repressive epigenetic marks.
claims.source: Surprisingly, quantification of the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions in D. melanogaster revealed that more than half of the euchromatic TEs analyzed are associated with at least 1 kb spread of repressive epigenetic marks, with an average spread of 4.5 kb from TEs that display epigenetic effects.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The average spread of repressive epigenetic marks is 4.5 kb from TEs that display epigenetic effects.
claims.source: Surprisingly, quantification of the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions in D. melanogaster revealed that more than half of the euchromatic TEs analyzed are associated with at least 1 kb spread of repressive epigenetic marks, with an average spread of 4.5 kb from TEs that display epigenetic effects.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Repressive DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs in A. thaliana predominantly spreads only a few hundred base pairs.
claims.source: In contrast, repressive DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs in A. thaliana predominantly spreads only a few hundred base pairs (Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in A. thaliana.

claims.claim: ~20% of the euchromatic genes are within 5 kb from at least one TE insertion in the reference D. melanogaster strain.
claims.source: Since ~20% of the euchromatic genes are within 5 kb from at least one TE insertion in the reference D. melanogaster strain (Kaminker et al., 2002; Quesneville et al., 2005; Hoskins et al., 2015), these estimates suggest that the epigenetic influence of TEs on functional sequences is extensive in D. melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genome annotation studies.

claims.claim: The epigenetic influence of TEs on functional sequences is extensive in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Since ~20% of the euchromatic genes are within 5 kb from at least one TE insertion in the reference D. melanogaster strain (Kaminker et al., 2002; Quesneville et al., 2005; Hoskins et al., 2015), these estimates suggest that the epigenetic influence of TEs on functional sequences is extensive in D. melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the proportion of genes near TEs and the extent of epigenetic spreading.

claims.claim: TEs contribute significantly to genic DMRs (differential methylated regions) between genomes in Arabidopsis.
claims.source: This concurs with observations in Arabidopsis that TEs contribute significantly to genic DMRs (differential methylated regions) between genomes (Schmitz et al., 2013; Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Arabidopsis.

claims.claim: TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes has been demonstrated in Drosophila.
claims.source: TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes has been demonstrated in Drosophila (Cridland et al., 2015; Lee 2015), and the spreading of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs is a plausible mechanism for such observations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The spreading of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs is a plausible mechanism for TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes.
claims.source: TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes has been demonstrated in Drosophila (Cridland et al., 2015; Lee 2015), and the spreading of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs is a plausible mechanism for such observations.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the observed epigenetic effects.

claims.claim: Recent studies that jointly analyzed mobilomes and transcriptomes in A. thaliana populations found that TE insertions result in equal frequencies of increased and decreased expression of flanking genes.
claims.source: In fact, recent studies that jointly analyzed mobilomes and transcriptomes in A. thaliana populations found that TE insertions result in equal frequencies of increased and decreased expression of flanking genes (Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in A. thaliana.

claims.claim: SNPs and copy number variants (CNVs) in regulatory sequences are identified as significant contributors to differential expression between homologous alleles.
claims.source: Besides, SNPs and copy number variants (CNVs) in regulatory sequences are also identified as significant contributors to differential expression between homologous alleles (Massouras et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks and heterochromatin proteins is high for active genes normally located in the pericentromeric heterochromatin, and is required for the proper expression of these genes.
claims.source: In fact, enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks and heterochromatin proteins is surprisingly high for active genes normally located in the pericentromeric heterochromatin, and is required for the proper expression of these genes (Wakimoto and Hearn, 1990; Hearn et al., 1991; Yasuhara and Wakimoto, 2008; Riddle et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There is a deficiency in the number of genes that both have adjacent TEs and are expressed in 4–8 hr embryos.
claims.source: In fact, we observed a deficiency in the number of genes that both have adjacent TEs and are expressed in 4–8 hr embryos (using data from modEncode (Graveley et al., 2011); Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.00017, odds ratio = 0.73).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claims.claim: The deficiency in genes with adjacent TEs that are expressed in 4–8 hr embryos is even stronger when only considering TEs with epigenetic effects.
claims.source: This deficiency is even stronger when only considering TEs with epigenetic effects (Fisher's Exact Test, p<10−5, odds ratio = 0.58).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Epigenetic marks established at embryonic stages are expected to influence both somatic and germline cells.
claims.source: Epigenetic marks established at embryonic stages are expected to influence both somatic and germline cells, and were experimentally demonstrated to have a long lasting functional effect through development (Gu and Elgin, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The observed deficiency in expressed genes with adjacent TEs is consistent with selection preferentially removing TEs that result in spreading of repressive epigenetic marks to adjacent genes expressed in embryonic stages.

results.result: More than half (54.2%) of euchromatic TEs in D. melanogaster are associated with spreading of repressive epigenetic marks (H3K9me2, H3K9me3, HP1a) to flanking sequences, extending an average of 4.5 kb and up to 20 kb. This spreading is caused by TE insertions rather than pre-existing epigenetic states, as demonstrated by comparing homologous sequences with and without TEs in two D. melanogaster strains (RAL315 and RAL360).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C39-C48, C95-C96 are strongly supported by ChIP-seq data from multiple strains and developmental stages (Figures 1-2). The comparison of homologous alleles with and without TEs (C44-C45) provides compelling evidence for causality. Quantitative measurements (C46-C48) are based on rigorous statistical analysis with appropriate controls and replication.

results.result: The epigenetic effects of TEs are not restricted to specific genomic contexts. TEs with H3K9me2 spreading are not concentrated near pericentromeric or subtelomeric heterochromatin, and local repeat density does not correlate with the presence or magnitude of epigenetic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by genomic distribution analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and statistical tests showing no correlation with repeat density (p=0.55, 0.81, 0.65). The analysis appropriately controls for proximity to heterochromatin by using conservative boundaries (0.5 Mb distal).

results.result: The epigenetic effects of TEs vary substantially among TE families. LTR-type TEs show significantly larger increases in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to other TE types (median 0.547 vs 0.352, p=0.00047). TE families targeted by more piRNAs exhibit more extensive H3K9me2 spreading, while no significant association was found with endo-siRNA targeting.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by comprehensive analysis across TE families (Figures 3-4, Table 1). Statistical tests are appropriate (Mann-Whitney U test, Spearman rank correlation). The lack of difference in piRNA amounts between LTR and non-LTR TEs (C56) strengthens the conclusion that piRNA correlation is not solely driven by TE type.

results.result: TE families with higher copy numbers have larger proportions of insertions with epigenetic effects, supporting the prediction that epigenetic effects depend on TE abundance through piRNA-mediated mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by correlation analysis (Table 1, p=0.0036) using population data from Kofler et al. 2015. The correlation remains significant after removing outlier families (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), demonstrating robustness. This result is consistent with the piRNA generation mechanism.

results.result: TEs with stronger epigenetic effects have lower population frequencies in the Zambian D. melanogaster population. Low-frequency TEs are more likely to exhibit H3K9me2 spreading (p=0.039, OR=1.58), show more extensive spreading (p=0.011), and result in larger increases in H3K9me2 enrichment (p=0.014). Significant negative correlations exist between TE population frequency and both extent (ρ=-0.15) and magnitude (ρ=-0.14) of epigenetic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by population genomic analysis of 197 Zambian genomes (Figure 5). Statistical tests are appropriate and significant. The use of the Zambian population is well-justified as the ancestral population with limited admixture. Multiple regression analyses (Table 2) controlling for TE family identity confirm the associations, addressing potential confounding.

results.result: Recombination rate does not explain the observed associations between TE epigenetic effects and population frequencies. Neither the presence of H3K9me2 spreading nor its extent/magnitude correlates with local recombination rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by statistical analyses showing no significant associations (p=0.83, 0.62, 0.55). This effectively rules out an alternative explanation for the population frequency patterns and strengthens the conclusion that selection against epigenetic effects drives the observed patterns.

results.result: TEs cause differential epigenetic states at homologous genic alleles. Genes with adjacent TEs have significantly higher H3K9me2 enrichment than homologous alleles without TEs, with the effect being stronger for genes near TEs with epigenetic effects. Genes near low-frequency TEs show significantly higher z-scores than those near high-frequency TEs (p=0.0019), and gene z-scores negatively correlate with TE population frequency (ρ=-0.18, p<10⁻³).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C67-C74 are supported by z-score analysis comparing homologous alleles (Figure 6). The use of z-scores appropriately normalizes for between-strain differences. The correlation between gene epigenetic state and TE population frequency (C73-C74) provides strong evidence linking epigenetic effects to selection. Statistical tests are appropriate and significant.

results.result: Within strains, H3K9me2 enrichment negatively correlates with transcript levels for genes within 10 kb of TEs (ρ=-0.35 and -0.33, p<10⁻¹⁶). There is an excess of genes showing the expected pattern (higher H3K9me2 and lower expression in TE-adjacent alleles), particularly for TEs with epigenetic effects. However, this pattern is mainly observed in RAL360, and no correlation exists between H3K9me2 z-scores and expression fold changes for genes with nearby TEs.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 present mixed evidence. While within-strain correlations (C75) are strong and significant, the between-strain analysis (C76-C80) shows strain-specific effects and lack of correlation for TE-adjacent genes. The authors acknowledge complexity, noting exceptions where TE-adjacent alleles have both higher H3K9me2 and higher expression. Additional experiments are needed to clarify the functional consequences of TE-induced epigenetic changes on gene expression.

results.result: D. simulans exhibits stronger epigenetic effects of TEs compared to D. melanogaster. While the extent of H3K9me2 spread does not differ significantly between species (p=0.67), D. simulans shows a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (p=0.013) and larger increases in relative H3K9me2 enrichment (p=0.035). This correlates with lower TE content in D. simulans.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C82-C90 are supported by comparative ChIP-seq analysis between species (Figure 8). Statistical tests are appropriate (paired Mann-Whitney U tests). The analysis is conservative, including only TE families with ≥2 insertions in both species. The correlation with lower TE content (C6, C82) is well-established in the literature and consistent with the observed stronger epigenetic effects.

results.result: D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats (ANOVA p=0.00013) and higher expression of Su(var) genes as a group (p<10⁻⁶) compared to D. melanogaster. Specifically, Su(var)3-9 shows significantly higher expression in D. simulans. These differences in PEV modifiers could account for the stronger epigenetic effects of TEs in D. simulans.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C91-C94 are supported by K-mer analysis (Figure 9A) and RNA-seq data (Figure 9B-C). The K-mer approach is validated by consistency with previous studies using orthogonal methods. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for Su(var) expression is appropriate. The mechanistic link to PEV is well-established in the literature, making the inference (C94) reasonable.

results.result: The epigenetic effects of TEs and host genetic factors modulating these effects play a critical role in TE evolution within and between species. Selection against TEs with stronger epigenetic effects contributes to TE population dynamics, and the association between TE abundance and epigenetic effects supports synergistic epistasis. Variation in host genetic environment (Su(var) expression, heterochromatic DNA content) influences TE evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C8-C9, C112, C115, C119 represent the main conclusions synthesized from multiple lines of evidence: population frequency analysis (C5), between-species comparisons (C115), and host genetic variation (C119). These conclusions are well-supported by the data presented, though they represent inferences from correlative evidence rather than direct experimental manipulation.

results.result: There is a deficiency of genes that both have adjacent TEs and are expressed in 4-8 hr embryos (p=0.00017, OR=0.73), which is stronger when considering only TEs with epigenetic effects (p<10⁻⁵, OR=0.58). This is consistent with selection preferentially removing TEs that spread repressive marks to genes expressed in embryonic stages, when epigenetic marks have long-lasting effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by statistical analysis using modEncode expression data. Fisher's Exact Tests are appropriate and highly significant. The inference (C109) is reasonable given that epigenetic marks established in embryos influence both somatic and germline cells (C108, supported by citation). This provides indirect evidence for selection against TEs with functional consequences.

results.result: The stronger epigenetic effects in D. simulans should lead to stronger selection removing TE insertions. If TE proliferation rates are similar between species, this could account for the lower genomic TE content in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are logical inferences from the observed stronger epigenetic effects in D. simulans, but they are speculative (C114 explicitly conditional on similar proliferation rates). The manuscript does not provide data on transposition rates in the two species. Additional experiments measuring TE proliferation rates and selection coefficients would be needed to fully support this conclusion.

results.result: Su(var)3-9 is a dosage-dependent PEV modifier (haploid suppressor, triploid enhancer), suggesting that changes in its transcript levels would result in quantitative differences in TE epigenetic effects. Variation in heterochromatic DNA amount and Su(var) expression provides a viable explanation for differences in TE epigenetic effects between D. melanogaster and D. simulans.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are supported by citation to previous work (C116) and the observed expression differences (C93). The inference (C117-C118) is reasonable given the known dosage-dependent effects and the observed correlations. However, this remains correlative evidence; experimental manipulation of Su(var) expression would provide stronger support.

results.result: Background and context claims establishing the nature of TEs, their deleterious effects, regulation by small RNAs, low population frequencies, and previous evidence for epigenetic effects in various organisms including Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C38 are background claims supported by extensive citations to established literature. These provide appropriate context for the study. The citations appear accurate and relevant based on the claims made.

results.result: Discussion claims comparing results to other organisms and providing context for interpretation. In A. thaliana, DNA methylation spreads only a few hundred base pairs from TEs, contrasting with the more extensive spreading in Drosophila. Approximately 20% of D. melanogaster genes are within 5 kb of a TE, suggesting extensive epigenetic influence.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 are discussion points supported by appropriate citations. The comparison to A. thaliana (C97) highlights the biological significance of the findings. The inference about extensive epigenetic influence (C99) is reasonable given the proportion of genes near TEs (C98) and the observed spreading distances.

results.result: Theoretical work predicts that stable TE equilibrium requires synergistic epistasis of deleterious effects. However, synergistic epistasis has only been empirically supported for ectopic recombination-mediated effects, not for other proposed deleterious mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by citations to theoretical (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1983) and empirical work (Langley et al., 1988; Petrov et al., 2003, 2011). These claims provide important context for the significance of finding evidence for synergistic epistasis through epigenetic effects (C112).

results.result: PEV is temperature sensitive and influenced by abiotic factors. Different environmental conditions in diverse habitats could contribute to variation in TE epigenetic effects and divergent TE profiles within and between species.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by citations. However, C122 is speculative, extending the findings to environmental variation without direct evidence. While the inference is reasonable given the environmental sensitivity of heterochromatin function, experimental data on environmental effects on TE epigenetics would be needed to support this claim.

results.result: Discussion of evolutionary mechanisms underlying between-species differences in PEV modifiers. The deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs are side effects of host silencing, making direct selection for stronger effects unlikely. Alternative explanations include selection on pleiotropic Su(var) functions or changes in heterochromatic DNA from other processes. TE evolution may be more tightly associated with other cellular/chromosomal processes than previously appreciated.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are discussion points appropriately supported by citations (C123, C125) and logical reasoning. The authors appropriately acknowledge alternative explanations (C126) and avoid overinterpreting their correlative data. The broad conclusion (C127) is a reasonable inference from the observed connections between TE evolution and host genetic factors.
